title: Rate Limiter
prompt: Design a rate limiter that enforces request quotas per client/user. Support multiple algorithms: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window, Sliding Window Log, and Sliding Window Counter. The RateLimiter interface should allow querying whether a request is allowed and should integrate with pluggable Clock (for testability) and Storage backends (in-memory vs distributed). Thread-safe and efficiently track state per unique key (user ID, IP address, etc.).

stages.title: Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: Clarify the requirements. What's in scope and what isn't?
stages.howToAnswer: Capture the rules tightly. Decide the algorithm scope (support all 5 or just one), limits per client, time windows, and storage strategy. State assumptions about concurrency and persistence.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Web Cache):
bullets: Cache GET requests with a time-to-live (TTL)
Evict stale entries on TTL expiry or LRU when full
Support both in-memory and Redis-backed storage
Out of Scope: distributed cache coordination, multi-node consistency

must: Single rate limiter instance enforces a quota: max N requests in M seconds per key
isAllowed(key) -> bool: returns whether a request is permitted
Support at least one algorithm (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window, Sliding Window Log, or Sliding Window Counter)
Thread-safe under concurrent requests
should: Support pluggable algorithms (strategy pattern)
Pluggable Clock for testability (not hard-coded System.currentTimeMillis)
Pluggable Storage (in-memory vs Redis-like backend)
Track per-key state independently
avoid: Designing a distributed consensus mechanism (keep it single-process or delegate to Storage)
UI or HTTP integration (focus on the core algorithm classes)
Automatically expiring old keys without explicit storage cleanup

stages.sampleAnswer:
Scope:
- Single RateLimiter instance. Constructor takes rate (requests per second/minute), window size in milliseconds, and algorithm type.
- isAllowed(key: str) -> bool: returns true if request is allowed, false if quota exceeded.
- Support Token Bucket as primary algorithm; extensible to others.
- Thread-safe: use synchronized blocks or ConcurrentHashMap per algorithm.
- In-memory Storage by default; pluggable Storage interface for Redis-like backends.
- Clock interface for testing (defaults to System.currentTimeMillis).

Out of scope:
- Distributed rate limiting (no cross-process consensus).
- HTTP response codes or middleware integration.
- Automatic key expiration (Storage is responsible for TTL if needed).
- Rate limiter for different tiers (e.g., free vs premium) — single quota per key.
hints: Rate limiting is about allowing N events per M seconds. Clarify: what's a 'request'? What identifies a client?
Pick one algorithm first (Token Bucket is intuitive). Then think about what seams let you swap other algorithms cleanly.
Thread-safety is critical: concurrent requests on the same key must serialize their state updates. How?

stages.title: Entities & Relationships
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core entities and how do they relate?
stages.howToAnswer: Pick the orchestrator (RateLimiter). Decide what owns the algorithm state (per-key buckets, counters, queues). Identify pluggable abstractions (Storage, Clock, RateLimitingAlgorithm).

must: RateLimiter (orchestrator): holds algorithm and storage, dispatches isAllowed(key)
RateLimitingAlgorithm (interface): defines the contract (isAllowed, updateState per algorithm type)
Storage (interface): stores per-key state (buckets, counters, timestamps)
should: Clock (interface): injection point for time, not System.currentTimeMillis
Concrete implementations: TokenBucketRateLimiter, LeakyBucketRateLimiter, FixedWindowRateLimiter, SlidingWindowLogRateLimiter, SlidingWindowCounterRateLimiter
Per-key locks or thread-safe map to serialize concurrent access to the same key
avoid: Putting all algorithm logic on RateLimiter itself; use strategy pattern
Hardcoding Storage to HashMap; inject via constructor

stages.sampleAnswer:
- RateLimiter (orchestrator): receives a rate limit config (max requests, window), algorithm type, Clock, and Storage. isAllowed(key) delegates to the algorithm's check method and updates state via Storage.
- RateLimitingAlgorithm (interface): abstract contract with isAllowed(key, currentTime, state) -> bool and updateState(key, currentTime, state) -> newState.
- Storage (interface): get(key) -> state, put(key, state) -> void. In-memory impl uses ConcurrentHashMap<String, PerKeyState>. Redis impl delegates to Lua script.
- Clock (interface): now() -> long. Defaults to System.currentTimeMillis().
- Per-key synchronization: RateLimiter maintains a lock per key (or a global lock for simplicity; trade-off between throughput and complexity).
hints: Identify the orchestrator: which class is called by the user? Which owns the algorithm and storage?
Rate limiter state is per-key: bucket for one user, separate bucket for another. How do you isolate them without a God class?
Clock is a seam: why inject it? (testability — you can fast-forward time in a unit test without waiting)

stages.title: Class Design
stages.questionPrompt: Define the classes — fields and methods. Keep algorithm logic separate from orchestration.
stages.howToAnswer: Sketch each class with explicit method signatures and what they return. Use enums for algorithm types. Constructor parameters: rate, window, algorithm, clock, storage.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Elevator):
bullets: class Elevator: + moveToFloor(floor) -> bool, + getCurrentFloor() -> int

must: interface RateLimitingAlgorithm: + isAllowed(key, currentTime, state) -> bool
class RateLimiter: + isAllowed(key: str) -> bool, constructor(rate, windowMs, algorithm, clock, storage)
interface Storage: + get(key) -> PerKeyState?, + put(key, state) -> void
Enum for algorithm types (TOKEN_BUCKET, LEAKY_BUCKET, etc.)
should: TokenBucketState: + tokens: double, + lastRefillTime: long
FixedWindowState: + count: long, + windowStart: long
SlidingWindowLogState: + timestamps: List<Long>
SlidingWindowCounterState: + currentCount: long, + prevCount: long, + windowStart: long
LeakyBucketState: + queue: Queue<Long>, + lastLeakTime: long
Clock interface: + now() -> long
avoid: Methods returning bare bool without context (ok, return the allow/deny decision clearly)
Hard-coded constants (rate, window size) — pass via constructor
Mixing algorithm logic with orchestration in one class

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
enum AlgorithmType { TOKEN_BUCKET, LEAKY_BUCKET, FIXED_WINDOW, SLIDING_WINDOW_LOG, SLIDING_WINDOW_COUNTER }

interface RateLimitingAlgorithm:
  isAllowed(key: str, currentTime: long, state: PerKeyState?) -> bool
  updateState(key: str, currentTime: long, state: PerKeyState?) -> PerKeyState

interface Storage:
  get(key: str) -> PerKeyState?
  put(key: str, state: PerKeyState) -> void

class RateLimiter:
  rate: int  // requests per window
  windowMs: long
  algorithm: RateLimitingAlgorithm
  clock: Clock
  storage: Storage
  keyLocks: ConcurrentHashMap<str, ReentrantLock>  // per-key synchronization
  
  constructor(rate, windowMs, algorithm, clock, storage):
    this.rate = rate
    this.windowMs = windowMs
    this.algorithm = algorithm
    this.clock = clock
    this.storage = storage
  
  isAllowed(key: str) -> bool:
    lock = getOrCreateLock(key)
    lock.lock()
    try:
      currentTime = clock.now()
      state = storage.get(key)
      allowed = algorithm.isAllowed(key, currentTime, state)
      if allowed:
        newState = algorithm.updateState(key, currentTime, state)
        storage.put(key, newState)
      return allowed
    finally:
      lock.unlock()

class TokenBucketRateLimiter implements RateLimitingAlgorithm:
  rate: double  // tokens per millisecond
  capacity: int
  
  constructor(requestsPerSecond, capacity):
    this.rate = requestsPerSecond / 1000.0
    this.capacity = capacity
  
  isAllowed(key: str, currentTime: long, state: TokenBucketState?) -> bool:
    if state == null:
      state = new TokenBucketState(capacity, currentTime)
    refill(state, currentTime)
    if state.tokens >= 1.0:
      return true
    return false
  
  updateState(key: str, currentTime: long, state: TokenBucketState?) -> TokenBucketState:
    if state == null:
      state = new TokenBucketState(capacity, currentTime)
    refill(state, currentTime)
    state.tokens -= 1.0
    return state
  
  refill(state: TokenBucketState, currentTime: long) -> void:
    elapsed = currentTime - state.lastRefillTime
    tokensToAdd = elapsed * rate
    state.tokens = min(state.tokens + tokensToAdd, capacity)
    state.lastRefillTime = currentTime

class TokenBucketState:
  tokens: double
  lastRefillTime: long

interface Clock:
  now() -> long

class SystemClock implements Clock:
  now() -> long:
    return System.currentTimeMillis()
```
hints: Separate algorithm logic from RateLimiter orchestration: use an interface and strategy pattern.
State changes must be atomic: read current state, check quota, update state. Lock per key to prevent race conditions.
Token Bucket state: tokens (double, not int, for fractional refills) and lastRefillTime. How do you refill on each check?

stages.title: Implementation
stages.questionPrompt: Pseudo-code the meaty methods and trace through one scenario.
stages.howToAnswer: Focus on the Token Bucket refill logic and the isAllowed check. Then trace a concrete sequence: first request at t=0, second at t=100ms, third at t=150ms with 10 req/sec capacity.

must: Token Bucket refill: elapsed time * rate, capped by capacity
isAllowed check: refill, decrement, update state atomically
Proper lock acquisition and release (no deadlock, exception-safe)
should: Trace through a concrete scenario with timestamps
Show handling of null state (first request ever on a key)
Demonstrate fractional token arithmetic (e.g., 50ms elapsed at 0.01 tokens/ms = 0.5 tokens added)
avoid: Integer arithmetic for tokens (loses precision)
Recomputing refill on every check without caching lastRefillTime
Forgetting to lock before reading and updating state

stages.sampleAnswer:
```
TokenBucketRateLimiter.refill(state, currentTime):
  elapsedMs = currentTime - state.lastRefillTime
  tokensToAdd = elapsedMs * rate  // e.g., 100ms * 0.01 tokens/ms = 1.0 token
  state.tokens = min(state.tokens + tokensToAdd, capacity)
  state.lastRefillTime = currentTime

RateLimiter.isAllowed(key):
  lock = keyLocks.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ReentrantLock())
  lock.lock()
  try:
    currentTime = clock.now()
    state = storage.get(key)
    allowed = algorithm.isAllowed(key, currentTime, state)
    if allowed:
      newState = algorithm.updateState(key, currentTime, state)
      storage.put(key, newState)
    return allowed
  finally:
    lock.unlock()
```

Trace: rate = 10 req/sec, capacity = 10 tokens.

Request 1 at t=0ms:
  state = null, create new TokenBucketState(tokens=10, lastRefillTime=0)
  refill: elapsed = 0, tokens = 10 + 0 = 10
  tokens >= 1.0 → allowed = true
  updateState: tokens = 10 - 1 = 9, lastRefillTime = 0
  storage.put(user1, state)
  return true

Request 2 at t=100ms:
  state = get from storage: TokenBucketState(tokens=9, lastRefillTime=0)
  refill: elapsed = 100 - 0 = 100ms, tokensToAdd = 100 * 0.01 = 1.0, tokens = min(9 + 1, 10) = 10
  tokens >= 1.0 → allowed = true
  updateState: tokens = 10 - 1 = 9, lastRefillTime = 100
  return true

Request 3 at t=150ms:
  state: TokenBucketState(tokens=9, lastRefillTime=100)
  refill: elapsed = 150 - 100 = 50ms, tokensToAdd = 50 * 0.01 = 0.5, tokens = min(9.5, 10) = 9.5
  tokens >= 1.0 → allowed = true
  updateState: tokens = 9.5 - 1 = 8.5, lastRefillTime = 150
  return true

(After 11 rapid requests, tokens = 0, next request blocked until refill happens.)
hints: The refill formula is elapsed * rate, capped by capacity. Why is it safe to cap? (Bucket cannot overflow beyond capacity.)
Per-key locks serialize state updates. Why not a global lock? (Throughput: concurrent requests to different keys can proceed in parallel.)
Trace a full scenario: initial state, refill, decrement, state persisted, next request resumes from that state.

stages.title: Extensibility
stages.questionPrompt: How would the design extend for: (1) supporting multiple algorithms (switch at runtime), (2) metrics/observability (track allow/deny counts), (3) distributed rate limiting (Redis backend)?
stages.howToAnswer: Stay high-level. Point at the seams in the design that make each change clean without rewriting core classes.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Tic Tac Toe):
bullets: N-in-a-row: Board already takes winLength, just pass 5 instead of 3
AI opponent: Player becomes an interface; HumanPlayer / AIPlayer impls
Networked play: introduce MoveSource (Local vs Websocket)

must: Multiple algorithms: RateLimiter already takes an algorithm parameter. Instantiate TokenBucket / LeakyBucket / FixedWindow as separate classes implementing RateLimitingAlgorithm. Switch at runtime by passing different instances.
should: Metrics: introduce an Observer interface (AllowDenyObserver) that RateLimiter notifies after each check. Default no-op; Prometheus impl counts allow/deny per key.
Distributed: Storage interface is already pluggable. Implement Storage with Redis client + Lua script. RateLimiter logic stays unchanged; algorithm state lives on the server, checked via Storage API.
avoid: Rewriting RateLimiter for each algorithm variant
Hard-coding metrics to a single backend
Mixing algorithm logic with distribution logic

stages.sampleAnswer:
Multiple algorithms:
RateLimiter constructor already takes RateLimitingAlgorithm. Create concrete classes: TokenBucketRateLimiter, LeakyBucketRateLimiter, FixedWindowRateLimiter, etc. Caller decides: `new RateLimiter(rate, window, new TokenBucketRateLimiter(...), clock, storage)`. No changes to RateLimiter itself.

Metrics/Observability:
Introduce interface Observer { onAllow(key, time), onDeny(key, time) }. RateLimiter maintains a list of observers. After each isAllowed check, call observer.onAllow or observer.onDeny. Prometheus impl tracks counters per algorithm and key. RateLimiter is unaware of metrics backend.

Distributed (Redis):
Storage interface is the seam. Implement RedisStorage { get(key) -> decode Lua result, put(key, state) -> encode state, call Redis EVAL }. Per-algorithm Lua scripts (token-bucket.lua, sliding-window-counter.lua) handle the state check+update atomically on the server. RateLimiter.isAllowed stays the same; all network logic hidden in Storage impl.
hints: Algorithms: your constructor already takes a RateLimitingAlgorithm. What's the minimal change to swap Token Bucket for Sliding Window Counter?
Metrics: after each allow/deny decision, notify observers. Does RateLimiter care who listens?
Distributed: the Storage interface is the boundary. On one side: in-memory HashMap. On the other: Redis + Lua. RateLimiter doesn't know the difference.

deepDives.title: Algorithm trade-offs
deepDives.questionPrompt: Token Bucket allows bursts up to capacity; Sliding Window Counter approximates sliding; Leaky Bucket enforces strict drain rate. When would you choose each? What are the trade-offs?
deepDives.sampleAnswer:
Token Bucket: allows bursts (up to capacity) while enforcing average rate. Best for APIs expecting bursty traffic (mobile app batching, database writes in bulk). Trade-off: requires floating-point math; over-generous to sudden bursts.

Sliding Window Counter: blends two fixed windows with a weighted average. Memory: 2 keys per client. Rare edge case where it over-allows slightly at window boundaries. Best for most APIs — good accuracy, low memory.

Sliding Window Log: records every request timestamp. Memory: O(n) per key (one timestamp per request). True sliding window, no approximation. Best for high-value APIs (payments, fraud detection) where exact fairness is critical and memory cost is acceptable.

Leaky Bucket (policing): rejects overflow immediately (FIFO queue drops excess). Strict no-burst behavior. Best for protecting backend services: hard guarantee that downstream never sees more than the drain rate.

Leaky Bucket (shaping): queues excess requests, drains at fixed rate. Adds latency but guarantees all requests eventually process (if queue doesn't overflow). Best for request smoothing, traffic shaping.

Fixed Window: simplest, lowest memory. Window boundary allows 2x burst (N req in last 1s of window + N req in first 1s of next window). Best for simple login throttling or coarse-grained limits.

must: Explain burst behavior of at least 2 algorithms
Trade-off: memory vs accuracy for at least 2 algorithms
should: Recommend algorithm for a specific use case (mobile, payment, backend protection)
Discuss Fixed Window's 2x boundary burst and why Sliding Window fixes it
avoid: Saying one algorithm is always best; they have different trade-offs
Confusing Leaky Bucket policing vs shaping modes

hints: Burst behavior: Token Bucket fills up when idle, Leaky enforces steady drain, Sliding Window Log never allows more than rate × window per any continuous interval. Which matches your use case?
Memory: Fixed Window / Token Bucket use O(1) per client. Sliding Window Log uses O(n). Which can you afford?
Test case: at time 0, 10 requests arrive. At time 1s, 10 more arrive. With 10 req/sec limit, which algorithms allow both batches? Which reject the first batch?

deepDives.title: Thread safety and correctness
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you ensure that concurrent requests to the same key don't cause race conditions or double-counting?
deepDives.sampleAnswer:
Shared state per key (tokens, counter, timestamps) must be read-updated atomically. Per-key locking (via ReentrantLock or synchronized on key-specific object) ensures that two concurrent requests on the same key serialize their state check+update:

1. Lock key X.
2. Read state from storage.
3. Refill (or recalculate counter).
4. Check quota.
5. Update state (decrement tokens or increment counter).
6. Persist to storage.
7. Unlock key X.

Without locking, Thread A and Thread B both read state with 1 token left, both see 'allowed', both decrement — state ends up at -1 instead of 0.

Alternative: atomic operations (AtomicLong for fixed-window counter) avoid explicit locks but only work for simple counters, not complex state (floating-point tokens, timestamps). For most algorithms, per-key locks are the clearest approach.

Distributed (Redis): use Lua scripts (EVAL or EVALSHA). Lua code runs atomically on the server, no client-side locks needed. Script reads state, checks quota, updates state — all in one Redis round trip.

must: Identify the shared state (tokens, counter, timestamps)
Explain why it must be atomic (read-check-update)
Concrete synchronization mechanism (per-key lock or Lua)
should: Trace a race condition scenario and show how locking prevents it
Discuss per-key vs global lock trade-off (throughput)
avoid: Sprinkling synchronized / lock everywhere without justification
Assuming storage.get() + algorithm.isAllowed() + storage.put() is atomic when it's not

hints: State = tokens (or counter, or timestamps). If two threads read simultaneously and both think there's quota, what goes wrong?
Lock granularity: lock per key (fine-grained, high throughput) vs global lock (coarse, simpler, lower throughput). Which for a rate limiter?
Distributed: Lua scripts on Redis replace per-key locks. Why is EVAL atomic? (Server executes script without interruption.)

deepDives.title: Distributed rate limiting
deepDives.questionPrompt: How does the design support a distributed backend (Redis) where state is shared across multiple servers?
deepDives.sampleAnswer:
Storage interface is the seam. RedisStorage.get(key) and put(key, state) delegate to Redis:

1. get(key) → HGETALL key (retrieve all fields of a hash: tokens, lastRefillTime for Token Bucket).
2. put(key, state) → HSET key field value (persist new state).

For true atomicity (no TOCTOU bugs), use Redis Lua scripting:

```
local state = redis.call('HGETALL', KEYS[1])
local tokens = tonumber(state.tokens or 10)
local lastRefillTime = tonumber(state.lastRefillTime or 0)
local currentTime = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])

local elapsed = currentTime - lastRefillTime
local tokensToAdd = elapsed * rate / 1000
tokens = math.min(tokens + tokensToAdd, 10)

if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens = tokens - 1
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'lastRefillTime', currentTime)
  return 1  -- allowed
else
  return 0  -- denied
end
```

Multiple servers call the same Redis Lua script with the same key; Redis guarantees serial execution of the script. State is not in-process; it's on the Redis server, shared across all clients.

Serialization: per-algorithm state struct must encode/decode to/from Redis Hash or String (JSON for complex types).

TTL: Redis EXPIRE or PEXPIRE on keys to auto-cleanup old clients (optional; depends on requirements).

must: Storage interface is the seam; RedisStorage impl swaps in for in-memory HashMap
Lua script for atomic read-check-update (no client-side locking)
Encoding state (tokens, counter, etc.) for transmission to Redis
should: Show Redis Lua script for Token Bucket algorithm
Discuss TTL for auto-cleanup
Mention that RateLimiter orchestration is unchanged; only Storage differs
avoid: Doing read-check-update in separate Redis calls (TOCTOU race)
Hardcoding algorithm logic in Redis script; prefer per-algorithm scripts as separate files

hints: State lives on Redis, not in your process. How does RedisStorage.get(key) and put(key, state) work?

Atomicity: if two servers call Redis for the same key, Redis Lua script ensures only one refills and decrements at a time. Why not use WATCH + MULTI + EXEC? (Lua is simpler, faster, single round trip.)
Per-algorithm Lua: Token Bucket script differs from Sliding Window script. How do you organize them (separate .lua files, loader in RedisStorage constructor)?
